This page documents the general design of fastreg. It covers some
requirements, the public-facing interface, and some diagrams
highlighting the general flow of the main functions.

## Requirements

The core requirements of fastreg are to:

1. Convert Danish register data from SAS files to the modern and
   efficient Parquet format.
2. Read register Parquet files into R as a DuckDB table.
3. Provide a [targets](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) pipeline
   template to convert multiple registers in parallel.
4. Provide functions to list available SAS or Parquet register files
   directly from R.

## Interface

The interface (the functions and objects that are exposed to users) is
based on some specific naming conventions. Specifically, we generally
name function by the **action** they perform and the **object(s)** they
perform it on in the format `{action}_{object}()`. **Actions** are verbs
that describe what a function does, while **objects** are nouns that
represent the objects that the functions operate on. Below is an
overview of the main actions and objects within fastreg.

The actions are:

- `convert`: Convert a register SAS file (or multiple) to Parquet.
- `list`: List files in a directory, e.g., SAS or Parquet files.
- `read`: Read a Parquet register into R as a DuckDB table.
- `use`: Use a template in the current project.

While the objects are:

- `chunk_size`: Number of rows to read per chunk during conversion.
- `path`: A character vector of one or more paths.
- `output_dir`: The directory to save the Parquet output to.

::: callout-tip
For a list of all the public functions, see the
[Reference](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/reference/index.html)
page.
:::

### Converting SAS files from a single register

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-flow
%%| fig-cap: "Expected workflow for converting SAS files from a single register using `convert_register()`."
%%| fig-alt: "A flowchart showing the expected flow of converting register SAS files to Parquet files."
flowchart TD
    identify_paths("Identify register path(s)<br>with list_sas_files(path)")
    path[/"path<br>[Character vector]"/]
    output_dir[/"output_dir<br>[Character scalar]"/]
    chunk_size[/"chunk_size<br>[Integer scalar]"/]
    convert_register("convert_register()")
    output[/"Parquet file(s)<br>written to output_dir"/]

    %% Edges
    identify_paths -.-> path --> convert_register
    output_dir & chunk_size --> convert_register
    convert_register --> output

    %% Style
    style identify_paths fill:#FFFFFF, color:#000000, stroke-dasharray: 5 5
```

### Converting multiple registers in parallel

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-targets-flow
%%| fig-cap: "Expected workflow for converting multiple registers using the targets pipeline."
%%| fig-alt: "A flowchart showing the expected flow of converting register SAS files to Parquet files using the provided targets pipeline template."
flowchart TD
    copy_pipeline("use_targets_template()")
    edit["Edit _targets.R as needed"]
    run_pipeline("targets::tar_make()")
    output[/"Parquet file(s)<br>written to directory<br>specified in _targets.R"/]

    %% Edges
    copy_pipeline --> edit --> run_pipeline --> output

    %% Style
    style edit fill:#FFFFFF, color:#000000, stroke-dasharray: 5 5
```

::: callout-warning
`convert_file()`, the core function behind converting SAS files to
Parquet and used within `convert_register()` and the targets template,
creates an Arrow schema with data types based on the first file chunk.
This means that data type schemas are defined *within* files only. As a
result, if there's a drift in data types across SAS files in the same
register, this may not be identified in the conversion process, but will
become evident when attempting to read the register.

We use this design to ensure that subsequent chunks follow the same schema
as the first, as we don't want to have different data types across chunks
of the same partition (e.g. `part-*.parquet`).
:::

### Reading a Parquet register

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-flow-use
%%| fig-cap: "Expected workflow for reading a Parquet register as a DuckDB table using `read_register()`."
%%| fig-alt: "A flowchart showing the expected flow of reading a Parquet register created with the fastreg package."
flowchart TD
    path[/"path<br>[Character scalar]"/]
    read_register("read_register()")
    output[/"Output<br>[DuckDB table]"/]

    %% Edges
    path --> read_register --> output

```

## Conversion report

The conversion report exists to give confidence that the resulting
Parquet dataset can be read correctly with `unify_schemas`. Because a
register is split into multiple Parquet part files (one per chunk), all
parts must have identical column names, types, and counts; any
discrepancy could cause columns to be silently dropped or read as the
wrong type when reading the full dataset.

This report addresses two overall checks:

1. That the column names and data types are identical for all Parquet
   partitions for a single register.
2. That the chunking and writing pipeline works correctly (checking that
   the data is *the same* if read from the SAS file and read in from the
   written Parquet file).

The "sameness" notion in the list above covers a row count, column name
comparison, and a comparison of a minimal set of statistics:

| Type            | Stats                           |
|-----------------|---------------------------------|
| Numeric         | sum, missing count              |
| Date/datetime   | sum (as integer), missing count |
| Character       | missing count                   |
| Logical         | sum, missing count              |
| Factor/labelled | missing count                   |

The report compares each SAS chunk against its corresponding Parquet
part. Since users also access data through R (or Python), R-to-R
comparisons are a helpful check: a dropped chunk will show up as a row
count mismatch, a corrupted value will show up as a stat difference.

Note that this report cannot guarantee that all SAS values are perfectly
preserved after conversion, since SAS file formats are proprietary, and
reading SAS files in R relies on `haven`, which is a reverse-engineered
effort to read in SAS in environments like R.

We coerce a SAS file's data types using a fixed Arrow schema by deriving
from the first chunk and apply this schema to all subsequent chunks,
ensuring consistent types across all part files. However, this only
ensures type alignment within chunks from a single SAS file. Since
fastreg outputs several SAS files into the same register dataset (e.g.,
`bef2020.sas7bdat` and `bef2021.sas7bdat` into the same `bef/` folder),
we also need to ensure that the data types are the same in the Parquet
files within the entire register (e.g., the `bef/` folder), so the
register can be read into R collectively.


Below is an example of how the report is structured:

```{.text filename="conversion-report-20260316-143022.txt"}
# Conversion report 2026-03-16 14:30:22


Each column is followed by [OK] or [DIFF]:
- [OK]: Checked statistics are identical in the SAS chunk and written
  Parquet file.
- [DIFF]: At least one stat differs. Expanded with SAS and Parquet side
  by side.

If you come across a problem, please report it at:
https://github.com/dp-next/fastreg/issues/new.

## lmdb2020.sas7bdat

### Chunk 1

Parquet file name: `lmdb/year=2020/d39f98.parquet`

Rows:

- SAS: 1000
- Parquet: 1000

| Variable | Status |
| --- | --- |
| pnr | OK |
| pnr | OK |
| atc | OK |
| apk | DIFF |

apk [double] [DIFF]
| --- | SAS | Parquet |
| min | 1.01 | 0.99 |
| mean | 5.51 | 5.49 |

### Chunk 2
...
```

Overview of the implementation of the conversion report:

- Report helper functions are be placed in `write-report.R`
- Report functions are called within `convert_file()` since both
  `convert_register()` and the targets template rely on that function.
- To lower the risk of workers writing at the same time (the target
  pipeline parallelises per *SAS file*), the report lines are collected
  for all chunks within a file before writing to the report.
- `initialise_report()` creates the report file
  `conversion_report_<datetime>.txt` in the beginning of
  `convert_file()`, before the repeat.
- We use the already existing `read_register_file()` to read the written
  Parquet file that will be compared to the chunk.
- `create_chunk_comparison()` returns the report of the current chunk,
  e.g., the "Chunk 1" section above, as a character vector.
- Chunk comparisons are collected in a list `chunk_comparisons` within
  the repeat loop.
- `write_file_report()` then takes `chunk_comparisons` and writes them
  to the conversion report starting with a level-2 header with the SAS
  file name.
- Potentially: The targets template includes a target that reports on
  whether any "[DIFF]" is found within the conversion report so users
  won't have to inspect the conversion report manually.
